summary: This Wikipedia-derived note covers several aspects of Philadelphia: its median household income and wealth disparities, its history from the late 1700s onward (federal relocation, African Methodist Episcopal Church founding, industrialization, Republican then Democratic political shifts), and its economy, population and housing statistics. It also describes the city's government structure and current officials, its street layout, arts venues, climate, water system, Greyhound bus hub status, pre-colonial and colonial Lenape and European settlement history, and telephone area codes.
one_line: Wikipedia overview of Philadelphia covering its income and economy, political history, government, Penn-planned street grid, arts venues, climate, water system, Lenape and Dutch-Swedish colonial history, and area codes.
key_facts: The Census Bureau reported Philadelphia's median household income in 2013 as $36,836, down 7.9 percent from $40,008 in 2008 (in 2013 dollars).
Society Hill residents had a median household income of $93,720, while one North Philadelphia district reported the lowest at $14,185.
The federal government moved to Washington, DC in 1800 with completion of the White House and Capitol, after the state government left Philadelphia in 1799.
Philadelphia's free black community founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church (AME), the first independent black denomination in the country, before 1800.
Philadelphia became the first major industrial city in the United States after construction of roads, canals, and railroads, following New York City surpassing it in population.
Philadelphia was chosen as the host city for the first Republican National Convention in 1856.
Roosevelt carried Philadelphia with over 60% of the vote in 1936, and the city has remained Democratic in every presidential election since.
Philadelphia's annualized unemployment rate was 7.8% in 2014, down from 10.0% the previous year, compared with a national average of 6.2%.
Jim Kenney, a Democrat, is the mayor, having replaced Michael Nutter, who served two terms from 2009 to January 2016.
The Philadelphia City Council has ten district members and seven at-large members, and the current council president is Darrell Clarke.

Penn's surveyor Thomas Holme created a grid plan for Center City, and Penn planned five public parks, including Centre Square, Franklin Square, Logan Square, Rittenhouse Square, and Washington Square.
The Academy of Music is described as the nation's oldest continually operating opera house, and the Walnut Street Theatre as America's oldest theatre.
The Philadelphia Water Department draws about 57 percent of its drinking water from the Delaware River and the balance from the Schuylkill River.
The Philadelphia Greyhound Terminal at 1001 Filbert Street was the second busiest Greyhound terminal in the United States in 2006, after the Port Authority Bus Terminal in New York.
Dutch settlers built Fort Nassau in 1623 on the Delaware River, and the Swedish colony of New Sweden was established at Fort Christina in 1638.
